label: Jainism
sub: The Agamas, the Tattvartha Sutra, and the Tamil Jain classics
meta: Mahavira traditionally 599–527 BCE (many scholars: c. 5th century BCE) · Svetambara canon fixed at Valabhi, c. 5th century CE
history: Jains regard their teaching as eternal, renewed in each cosmic age by 24 Tirthankaras (“ford-makers”); the last, Mahavira, is traditionally dated 599–527 BCE, though many scholars place him about a century later, as a near-contemporary of the Buddha. His teachings were transmitted orally. The Svetambara sect's canon, the Agamas, was compiled at a final council at Valabhi in Gujarat around 453 or 466 CE, after earlier recitations. The Digambara sect holds that the original canon was lost, relying instead on works such as the Shatkhandagama and the Prakrit treatises attributed to Kundakunda. The Tattvartha Sutra (c. 2nd–5th century CE), the oldest Jain treatise in Sanskrit, is accepted by both.
impact: Jainism is especially relevant to this book: Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions in Tamil Nadu caves, among the oldest Tamil writing, record stone beds carved for Jain monks, and Jain authors produced classics such as the Naladiyar and the epic Jivaka Chintamani. Whether Thiruvalluvar was himself a Jain remains debated — some scholars point to the Kural's ethics of non-harm and vegetarianism, while others cite its references to a creator God. Today there are roughly 4–5 million Jains, about 4.5 million of them in India (2011 census). Jain ahimsa shaped Gandhi's nonviolence through his Jain mentor Shrimad Rajchandra, and Jain ethics continue to inform vegetarian and animal-welfare thought.
principles: At the center is ahimsa, non-harming of every living being, since all life, even plants and the smallest creatures, is held to possess a soul (jiva). Karma is understood literally as fine matter that binds to the jiva through passion and action, and liberation comes by stopping its inflow and wearing it away. The path is the “three jewels”: right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct. Conduct is framed by five vows — non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, chastity, and non-possession (aparigraha) — taken fully by monks and in moderated form by laypeople. Anekantavada, “many-sidedness,” teaches that no single viewpoint captures the whole truth. Jainism denies a creator God; the universe is uncreated and eternal.
